The CO-CHAIRS OF THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL NEGOTIATING BODY TO DRAFT AND 
NEGOTIATE A WHO CONVENTION, AGREEMENT OR OTHER INTERNATIONAL INSTRUMENT ON 
PANDEMIC PREVENTION, PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE, speaking in turn, said that the 
coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic had served as a reminder that no country could address 
a global health crisis alone and had shown what countries could achieve by working together. The 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body had been committed to an inclusive, open and transparent 
negotiating process, and its work had been guided by a shared conviction that health was a 
common good. 

The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement was the product of 13 formal rounds of negotiations 
across more than three years, with written submissions, public hearings, informal meetings and 
extensive consultations. Divergent opinions on key policy issues had not prevented Member States 
from reaching a consensus. Covering prevention, preparedness and response, the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement represented a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape global health 
and was intended to create a rules-based, future-proof system. It would bolster international 
cooperation on prevention through a One Health approach and scientific collaboration, with a 
focus on research, development and data sharing. It would not undermine national sovereignty 
and would guarantee equitable access to health products in the event of a pandemic. It would also 
strengthen health systems through, inter alia, investment in human resources and the promotion 
of technology transfer, while the establishment of a conference of the parties would ensure clear 
governance. Following the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, negotiations on the 
annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system would be undertaken by an 
intergovernmental working group prior to the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly. 

The representative of SOUTH AFRICA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the 
African Region, said that the COVID-19 pandemic had highlighted vulnerabilities in the global 
health architecture, particularly in terms of inequitable access to essential health products and 
technologies. The Member States of the African Region were therefore unwavering in their 
commitment to equity-driven efforts to address the disproportionate impacts of pandemics.
